goals: Explain what Directive Principles of State Policy are and why the framers included them
Name the Part and the Articles in which they are found and the source of the idea
Classify principles into socialistic, Gandhian and liberal-intellectual groups with examples
Explain why they are non-justiciable yet fundamental in the governance of the country

slides.heading: Directive Principles of State Policy
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the **goals** the Constitution sets for every government.

Examples in each group

visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: India became free in 1947 and its Constitution came into force in 1950. Freedom was only the beginning. People still needed food, work, schools and fair treatment. In this part we study the Directive Principles, the goals the framers set for every government to work toward, and how they are grouped.

slides.heading: Two Parts, two jobs
slides.body_md: The Constitution protects people through **rights** and guides governments through **principles**.

visual.alt: Table: Part III (Articles 12 to 35) holds the Fundamental Rights and can be enforced in court; Part IV (Articles 36 to 51) holds the Directive Principles and cannot be enforced in court

slides.narration: Part Three of the Constitution holds the Fundamental Rights, from Article twelve to thirty five. Part Four holds the Directive Principles of State Policy, from Article thirty six to fifty one. Rights can be enforced by courts. Principles are directions to the State. Keeping these two Parts apart is the key to this chapter.

slides.heading: What are Directive Principles?
bullets: Directions to the **State**: Parliament, State legislatures and governments.
Found in **Part IV**, Articles **36 to 51**.
The idea came from the **Irish Constitution**.
They aim at **social and economic justice**.

nodes.label: Idea from Ireland
Written into Part IV
Addressed to the State

visual.alt: Flow: the idea comes from the Irish Constitution, is written into Part IV and is addressed to the State
visual.caption: Where the idea came from.

slides.narration: Directive Principles of State Policy are directions to the State. The word State here means Parliament, State legislatures and governments. They are found in Part Four, Articles thirty six to fifty one. The framers took the idea from the Irish Constitution. Their purpose is to bring about social and economic justice.

slides.heading: Why were they included?
slides.body_md: Political freedom had to be followed by **fairness in daily life**.

nodes.label: Framers set goals in Part IV
Governments use them in laws and policies
Citizens judge performance at elections

visual.alt: Flow: the framers set goals in Part IV, governments use them in making laws and policies, and citizens judge performance at elections
visual.caption: Why they were included.

slides.narration: The framers knew that the vote alone would not remove hunger, poverty or unequal chances. So they set goals in Part Four. Governments use these goals when they make laws and policies. Citizens can then judge how well a government has done, especially at election time. The principles act as a compass for the country.

visual.alt: Three boxes of Directive Principles. Socialistic (economic): adequate livelihood, equal pay for equal work, right to work and public aid, living wage and humane work, resources for the common good. Gandhian: village panchayats, cottage industries, weaker sections including the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, prohibition of intoxicants, cow and cattle protection. Liberal-intellectual: uniform civil code, judiciary apart from the executive, protect monuments, international peace, environment under Article 48A
visual.caption: A teaching classification; the Constitution itself does not use these group names.

slides.narration: To study the principles easily, we sort them into three groups. Socialistic or economic principles deal with livelihood, work and wages. Gandhian principles deal with villages, small industries and weaker sections. Liberal-intellectual principles deal with matters such as the courts, heritage, peace and the environment. The Constitution itself does not use these group names.

slides.heading: Socialistic or economic principles

rows: Adequate means of livelihood for all citizens
Resources shared so that they serve the common good
Equal pay for equal work for men and women
Right to work and public assistance in unemployment, old age and sickness
Just and humane conditions of work; maternity relief
A living wage and a decent standard of life for workers

visual.alt: Table of socialistic or economic Directive Principles with the Article number of each: livelihood, common good, equal pay, right to work and public assistance, humane work and maternity relief, and a living wage

slides.narration: The first group aims at economic fairness. The State should secure adequate means of livelihood for all, share resources so that they serve the common good, and make sure men and women get equal pay for equal work. It should also provide the right to work, public assistance in old age, sickness and unemployment, humane working conditions and a living wage.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: sorting imagined schemes
slides.body_md: Name the principle behind a scheme first, then its group.
bullets: Step 1 — Read the scheme and ask what it does.
Step 2 — Match it to a principle.
Step 3 — Place the principle in its group.
Step 4 — Write the answer with a short reason.

rows: Loans and workshops for village potters
Allowance for the elderly with no support
Separate courts replace magistrates who judge and investigate

visual.alt: Table sorting three imagined schemes: loans for potters are Gandhian, an allowance for the elderly is socialistic, and separate courts are liberal-intellectual

slides.narration: Here is a simple method. Read the scheme and ask what it does. Match it to a principle. Then name the group. Loans for village potters follow the principle of cottage industries, which is Gandhian. An allowance for lonely old people follows public assistance in old age, which is socialistic. Separate courts follow the separation of the judiciary from the executive.

slides.heading: Gandhian principles

rows: Organise village panchayats as units of self-government
Promote cottage industries in rural areas
Promote the interests of weaker sections, including the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes
Prohibit intoxicating drinks and drugs injurious to health, except for medicinal use
Organise agriculture and animal husbandry on modern lines; protect cows, calves and other cattle

visual.alt: Table of Gandhian Directive Principles with the Article number of each: village panchayats, cottage industries, weaker sections, prohibition of intoxicants except for medicine, and agriculture with cattle protection

slides.narration: The Gandhian group reflects ideas of village self-rule and simple living. It includes organising village panchayats, promoting cottage industries, promoting the interests of weaker sections including the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and prohibiting intoxicating drinks except for medicinal use. It also speaks of modern agriculture and the protection of cows, calves and other cattle, stated here as a principle of the Constitution.

slides.heading: Liberal-intellectual principles

rows: A uniform civil code for citizens: the State is directed to endeavour towards it
Separate the judiciary from the executive
Protect monuments and places of national importance
Protect and improve the environment, forests and wildlife (added 1976)

visual.alt: Table of liberal-intellectual Directive Principles with the Article number of each: uniform civil code as a stated goal, separation of the judiciary from the executive, protection of monuments, international peace, and the environment added in 1976

slides.narration: The third group includes a uniform civil code, where the Constitution only directs the State to endeavour towards one. It also includes keeping the judiciary separate from the executive, protecting monuments of national importance, promoting international peace, and protecting the environment. This last principle, Article forty eight A, was added in 1976 by the forty second Amendment.

slides.heading: Non-justiciable but fundamental
bullets: **Non-justiciable:** a court cannot enforce them.
**Fundamental in governance:** the State must keep them in view when making laws.
Citizens can **judge** governments by them.

nodes.label: Citizen asks the court to order the State to act on a Directive Principle
Court: not justiciable, cannot compel
Citizen turns to the legislature, the government and elections

visual.alt: Flow: a citizen asks a court to enforce a Directive Principle; the court says it is non-justiciable and cannot compel; the citizen then turns to the legislature, the government and elections
visual.caption: What non-justiciable means in practice.

slides.narration: Non-justiciable means that a court cannot order the State to carry out a principle. Yet the Constitution says the principles are fundamental in the governance of the country, and it is the duty of the State to apply them when making laws. So a citizen cannot win a court order, but can press the legislature and the government, and can use elections.

(ii) One named group and one example per mark.
(iii) Reason for non-justiciable + the State's duty + citizens judge governments.
Aim for one point per mark.

Part three is the reason, the duty of the State, and how citizens judge governments.

slides.narration: To sum up: the Directive Principles are in Part Four, Articles thirty six to fifty one, and the idea came from Ireland. They direct the State toward social and economic justice. They fall into socialistic, Gandhian and liberal-intellectual groups. No court enforces them, yet governments are expected to follow them in making laws.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1
bullets: Write **Part IV, Articles 36 to 51**; do not mix with Part III (12 to 35).
Give an example with each group: do not just list the group names.
Say **non-justiciable** and explain it: courts cannot enforce them.
Do not quote the Articles; paraphrase their meaning.
For a classification question, name the principle first and then the group.
slides.narration: Some exam habits. Keep Part Four and Part Three apart, with their Article numbers. When you name a group, add an example. When you write non-justiciable, explain that courts cannot enforce the principle. You need not quote any Article; state its idea in your own words. And always name the principle before the group.

slides.narration: In this part we compare Fundamental Rights with Directive Principles, see how they work together, and learn what a welfare state is. We end with dated examples of laws that carry out the principles, such as the one on panchayats and the one on education.

slides.heading: Rights and principles side by side

rows: Society as a whole, over time

visual.alt: Table comparing Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles on part and articles, enforceability, nature, aim and who benefits

slides.narration: Fundamental Rights are in Part Three and can be enforced by courts, so they are justiciable. Directive Principles are in Part Four and cannot be enforced, so they are non-justiciable. Rights mostly limit what the State may do. Principles ask the State to act. Rights secure political democracy, while principles aim at social and economic democracy.

slides.heading: What justiciable means in practice
slides.body_md: A right can take a citizen to court; a principle cannot.

nodes.label: Right violated by the State
Citizen approaches the Supreme Court or a High Court
Court can order a remedy or strike down the law

visual.alt: Flow for a Fundamental Right: the right is violated by the State, the citizen approaches the Supreme Court or a High Court, and the court can order a remedy or strike down the law
visual.caption: A Fundamental Right can be enforced.

slides.narration: If the State violates a Fundamental Right, the citizen can approach the Supreme Court or a High Court. The court can order a remedy, or strike down a law that violates the right. No such path exists for a Directive Principle. That is the practical meaning of justiciable and non-justiciable.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: right or principle?
slides.body_md: Sort each imagined situation, and give the reason.
bullets: Step 1 — Ask: is a person being stopped or denied something the Constitution guarantees?
Step 2 — If yes, it is a **Fundamental Right**, enforceable in court.
Step 3 — If it is a goal for the State to pursue, it is a **Directive Principle**.
Step 4 — Write the reason: enforceable or not.

rows: Police stop a peaceful meeting with no lawful reason
Court can enforce freedom of assembly
The government plans elected village councils
A goal for the State; court cannot compel
A student is refused admission only because of caste
Equality can be enforced by a court

visual.alt: Table sorting three imagined situations: police stopping a peaceful meeting is a Fundamental Right issue, planning elected village councils is a Directive Principle, and refusing admission only because of caste is a Fundamental Right issue

slides.narration: Use a two step test. First ask whether someone is being stopped or denied something the Constitution guarantees. If so, it is a Fundamental Right, and a court can enforce it. If instead it is a goal for the State to work toward, it is a Directive Principle. Then write the reason: enforceable, or not enforceable.

slides.heading: Rights and principles complete each other
slides.body_md: A hungry person cannot enjoy freedom fully.

nodes.label: Fundamental Rights: political democracy
Directive Principles: social and economic democracy
Together: a fuller democracy and a welfare state

visual.alt: Flow: Fundamental Rights give political democracy, Directive Principles aim at social and economic democracy, and together they lead toward a fuller democracy and a welfare state
visual.caption: Rights and principles complete each other.

slides.narration: Rights and principles are partners. Fundamental Rights give freedom and equality, which is political democracy. Directive Principles aim at fair living conditions, which is social and economic democracy. A person who is hungry or out of school cannot use freedom fully. Together, rights and principles lead toward a fuller democracy and a welfare state.

slides.heading: What is a welfare state?
bullets: The government takes **responsibility for the well-being** of all citizens.
It provides **services**, offers **security** and works to **reduce inequality**.
It goes beyond the **night-watchman** role of law and order.

sections.heading: 1. Meaning, place and purpose
sections.body_md:
- **Directive Principles of State Policy** are directions given to the **State** (Parliament, State legislatures, governments) for making laws and policies.
- Placed in **Part IV**, **Articles 36 to 51**. The idea was borrowed from the **Irish Constitution**.
- **Purpose:** political freedom had to be matched by **social and economic justice**; the principles set the goals and let citizens judge governments.
- **Article 37:** not enforceable by any court, yet fundamental in the governance of the country; it is the **duty of the State** to apply them in making laws.
- Study is **elementary**: know the idea of each principle and the Article number; you need not quote the text.

Parliament, State legislatures and governments at the Union and State levels.

- **Liberal-intellectual:** uniform civil code, separation of the judiciary from the executive, protection of monuments, international peace, environment (Article 48A, added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976).

sections.heading: 4. Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles compared
sections.body_md:
- **Part and Articles:** rights in Part III (12 to 35); principles in Part IV (36 to 51).
- **Enforceability:** rights are **justiciable**; principles are **non-justiciable**.
- **Nature:** rights mostly **limit the State**; principles call for **positive action**.
- **Aim:** rights give **political democracy**; principles aim at **social and economic democracy**.
- **Courts:** a law violating a right can be struck down; a law is not struck down merely for not carrying out a principle.
- A claim in court rests on a **right**; a goal pursued by the government rests on a **principle**.

sections.heading: 5. Working together
sections.body_md:
- Rights and principles **complement** each other: freedom and equality need a base of food, work and education.
- **Example:** the right to education (Article 21A) and the principle of free and compulsory education aim at the same end.
- Governments act on the principles through **laws, budgets and schemes**; citizens press for them through the **legislature**, **public debate** and **elections**.

sections.heading: 6. The welfare state
sections.body_md:
- A **welfare state** takes responsibility for the **well-being** of all citizens, especially the poor and weak.
- It goes beyond a **night-watchman state** (law and order, defence, courts) by adding **health, education, social security** and measures that **reduce inequality**.
- The **Preamble** promises justice (social, economic, political); **Part IV** turns this into goals.
- **Dated examples:** Equal Remuneration Act (1976); 42nd Amendment (1976, Article 48A); 73rd Amendment (1992, panchayats); 86th Amendment (2002, Article 21A) and the Right to Education Act (2009); the rural employment guarantee Act of 2005 (right to work).
- Laws alone do not finish the task: **enforcement**, **resources** and **public awareness** matter.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Mixing up Part III (rights, 12 to 35) with Part IV (principles, 36 to 51).
- Writing that courts can enforce Directive Principles.
- Listing group names without examples.
- Quoting Articles instead of explaining their idea.
- Linking laws to the wrong principle or leaving out the year.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: one correct option, term or Article range.
- 2 marks: two distinct points; 3 marks: three points.
- 10-mark questions in 3 + 3 + 4 parts: one clear point per mark; the last part usually needs a reason, a link or an evaluation.

questions.stem_md: Under which Part of the Constitution of India are the Directive Principles of State Policy placed?

options.text_md: Part III
Part IV
Part II
Part V

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Part IV. The Directive Principles form Part IV, running from Article 36 to Article 51. Part III holds the Fundamental Rights, Part II deals with citizenship, and Part V deals with the Union government.

questions.stem_md: Which range of Articles makes up the Directive Principles of State Policy?

options.text_md: Articles 12 to 35
Articles 1 to 11
Articles 52 to 78
Articles 36 to 51

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Articles 36 to 51. Articles 36 to 51 are the Directive Principles. Articles 12 to 35 are the Fundamental Rights; Articles 1 to 11 deal with the Union and citizenship; Articles 52 to 78 deal with the President and the Union executive.

questions.stem_md: The idea of placing Directive Principles in a constitution was taken by the framers of the Indian Constitution from the constitution of which country?

options.text_md: Ireland
Canada
Japan
Switzerland

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Ireland. The framers were inspired by the Irish Constitution, which listed principles of social policy to guide its legislature. The other countries are not the source of this idea.

questions.stem_md: Why did the framers include Directive Principles in a Constitution of a country that had just become free?

options.text_md: To list the punishments for breaking the law
To fix the dates of elections in every State
To give governments goals for building a society with social and economic justice
To give courts the power to run the government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** To give governments goals for building a society with social and economic justice. The framers wanted political freedom to be followed by social and economic justice, so Part IV sets goals for law-makers and governments. It does not list punishments or election dates, and it does not hand administration to the courts.

questions.stem_md: When the Directive Principles are described as non-justiciable, what does this mean?

options.text_md: They have no importance in making laws
They apply only to the Union government and not to States
A court cannot order the government to carry them out
They can be changed by any State legislature

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A court cannot order the government to carry them out. Non-justiciable means not enforceable in a court of law. Article 37 says the principles are nonetheless fundamental in the governance of the country, so they are important, they apply to States too, and a State legislature cannot rewrite them.

questions.stem_md: Residents of the imagined district of Belapur file a petition asking the High Court to order their State to open a cottage-industry centre within a month, relying only on a Directive Principle. What is the most likely result?

options.text_md: The court cannot compel the State to act on a Directive Principle, which is left to the legislature and the government
The court orders the centre to be built, because Directive Principles are enforceable like rights
The court dissolves the State legislature for neglecting the principle
The court transfers the matter to the Election Commission

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The court cannot compel the State to act on a Directive Principle, which is left to the legislature and the government. Directive Principles are non-justiciable, so no court can compel their implementation; the State is expected to act through laws, budgets and policies. A court cannot dissolve a legislature, and the Election Commission does not hear such cases.

questions.stem_md: The imagined government of Sundarpur gives loans and workshop space to weavers and potters in its villages. Which group of Directive Principles does this policy mainly follow?

options.text_md: Socialistic principles
Liberal-intellectual principles
Principles of defence and security
Gandhian principles

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Gandhian principles. Encouraging cottage industries in rural areas is a Gandhian principle. Socialistic principles deal with livelihood and wages, liberal-intellectual ones with matters such as the judiciary and peace, and there is no group on defence.

questions.stem_md: An imagined State orders that women and men doing the same work in its tile factories must receive the same pay. Which Directive Principle is being put into effect?

options.text_md: Organising village panchayats, a Gandhian principle
Equal pay for equal work, a socialistic principle
Separation of the judiciary from the executive
Promotion of international peace

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Equal pay for equal work, a socialistic principle. Equal pay for men and women for equal work is a socialistic (economic) principle under Article 39. Village panchayats are Gandhian, and the other two options are liberal-intellectual principles that do not concern wages.

questions.stem_md: A newly formed imagined State decides that district magistrates will no longer both investigate cases and judge them, and sets up separate courts. Which group of Directive Principles does this belong to?

options.text_md: Liberal-intellectual principles
Gandhian principles
Socialistic principles
None, because it concerns only Fundamental Rights

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Liberal-intellectual principles. Separating the judiciary from the executive (Article 50) is a liberal-intellectual principle. It is not Gandhian or socialistic, and it is a Directive Principle, not a Fundamental Right.

questions.stem_md: A Directive Principle on protecting and improving the environment, forests and wildlife was not in the original Constitution of 1950. When and by which amendment was it added?

options.text_md: In 1951 by the First Amendment, as Article 40
In 1976 by the 42nd Amendment, as Article 48A
In 1992 by the 73rd Amendment, as Article 44
In 2002 by the 86th Amendment, as Article 51

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** In 1976 by the 42nd Amendment, as Article 48A. Article 48A came with the 42nd Amendment of 1976. The First Amendment of 1951 did not add it, the 73rd Amendment of 1992 concerned panchayats, and the 86th Amendment of 2002 concerned education.

questions.stem_md: The imagined State of Nilgiri Vale starts a monthly allowance for elderly persons who have no family support and no income. Which Directive Principle does this scheme support?

options.text_md: Protection of ancient monuments
Separation of the judiciary from the executive
Public assistance in old age, a socialistic principle
Prohibition of intoxicating drinks

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Public assistance in old age, a socialistic principle. Article 41 asks the State to make effective provision for public assistance in cases such as old age, sickness and unemployment; it is a socialistic (economic) principle. The other options concern heritage, the courts and public health.

questions.stem_md: A student lists four Directive Principles under the heading Gandhian. Which item has been placed in the wrong group?

options.text_md: Organising village panchayats as units of self-government
Encouraging cottage industries in rural areas
Promoting the interests of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes
Promoting international peace and friendly relations between nations

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Promoting international peace and friendly relations between nations. International peace (Article 51) is a liberal-intellectual principle. Village panchayats, cottage industries and the interests of weaker sections such as the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes are commonly grouped as Gandhian.

questions.stem_md: To whom are the Directive Principles of State Policy addressed?

options.text_md: Only to the Supreme Court
Only to the citizens of India
Only to the President
To the State: the legislatures and governments at the Union and State levels

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** To the State: the legislatures and governments at the Union and State levels. The principles are directions to the State, meaning Parliament, State legislatures and governments, to be kept in mind when making laws and policies. They are not orders addressed to the Supreme Court, to citizens alone, or to one office-holder.

questions.stem_md: Article 37 says that Directive Principles cannot be enforced by courts but are nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country. What is the best reading of the second part?

options.text_md: Courts must reject every law that does not follow them
Citizens may refuse to obey laws that ignore them
Governments are expected to keep the principles in view whenever they make laws and policies
They override every Fundamental Right

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Governments are expected to keep the principles in view whenever they make laws and policies. The Constitution places a duty on the State to apply the principles in making laws, even though the courts do not enforce them. It does not make laws void for ignoring them, allow disobedience, or give them priority over Fundamental Rights.

questions.stem_md: The Directive Principles of State Policy are contained in Part ___ of the Constitution.
questions.solution_md: They are contained in Part IV, Articles 36 to 51.

questions.stem_md: The framers of the Constitution drew the idea of Directive Principles from the constitution of ___.
questions.solution_md: The idea came from the Irish Constitution.

questions.stem_md: Article 48A, which asks the State to protect the environment, was added by the ___ Amendment in 1976.
questions.solution_md: It was added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976.

questions.stem_md: Match each Article of Part IV with the subject it deals with.

options.text_md: Article 40
Article 44
Article 48A
Article 50

match_right.text_md: A uniform civil code for citizens
Separation of the judiciary from the executive
Protection of the environment, forests and wildlife

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Article 40 concerns village panchayats, Article 44 a uniform civil code (the Constitution only directs the State to endeavour towards it), Article 48A the environment, and Article 50 the separation of the judiciary from the executive.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Citizens of an imagined State cannot go to court to force its government to carry out a Directive Principle immediately.

**Reason (R):** Directive Principles are non-justiciable.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true. Because the principles are non-justiciable, a court cannot enforce them, which is exactly why such a petition cannot succeed on that basis alone.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Directive Principle on protecting the environment, forests and wildlife formed part of the Constitution when it came into force in 1950.

**Reason (R):** Article 48A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment in 1976.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is false: the principle was added later. R is true: Article 48A came in 1976 through the 42nd Amendment.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Directive Principles of State Policy are placed in Part IV of the Constitution.

**Reason (R):** Directive Principles can be enforced by filing a writ petition in the Supreme Court.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true: Part IV, Articles 36 to 51. R is false: Directive Principles are non-justiciable, so they cannot be enforced through a writ petition.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A citizen can ask the Supreme Court to enforce a Directive Principle in the same way as a Fundamental Right.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Directive Principles are non-justiciable. Fundamental Rights can be enforced by the Supreme Court and the High Courts; Directive Principles cannot.

questions.stem_md: True or false? When the imagined State of Karuvan passes a law to provide free midday meals in schools, it may justify the law by pointing to the duty of the State to improve nutrition and public health.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Article 47 asks the State to raise the level of nutrition and improve public health, and Article 37 makes applying such principles in law-making a duty. A State may therefore cite the principle in support of its measure.

questions.stem_md: What are the Directive Principles of State Policy? Mention the Part and the Articles in which they are found.
questions.solution_md: Meaning, then Part and Articles.

answer.model_answer_md: They are **guidelines to the State** (governments and legislatures) for making laws and policies that bring about social and economic justice. They are found in **Part IV**, **Articles 36 to 51**.

marking_scheme.step: Meaning: guidelines for law-making and policy

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why the framers placed Directive Principles in the Constitution although courts cannot enforce them.
questions.solution_md: Any two sound reasons.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. After independence, **political freedom** needed to be followed by **social and economic justice**, so goals were set for governments.
2. The principles give **direction** to every future government and let citizens **judge its performance**.

questions.stem_md: Name any two Directive Principles that relate to the economic welfare of citizens.
questions.solution_md: Any two economic or socialistic principles.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The right of all citizens to **adequate means of livelihood**.
2. **Equal pay for equal work** for men and women. (Also: right to work, public assistance, a living wage, just and humane conditions of work.)

questions.stem_md: State two Directive Principles that are commonly called Gandhian.
questions.solution_md: Any two Gandhian principles.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Organising **village panchayats** as units of self-government (Article 40).
2. Encouraging **cottage industries** in rural areas. (Also: promoting the interests of weaker sections, and the prohibition of intoxicating drinks except for medicinal use.)

questions.stem_md: What does non-justiciable mean? Explain with reference to the Directive Principles.
questions.solution_md: Meaning, then its application to Part IV.

answer.model_answer_md: **Non-justiciable** means that a matter cannot be **enforced in a court of law**. A citizen cannot go to court to **compel** the State to carry out a Directive Principle, although the principles remain **fundamental in governance**.

marking_scheme.step: Cannot be enforced by a court
Applied to Directive Principles; still fundamental in governance

questions.stem_md: In the imagined State of Dhanora (a) police stop a peaceful public meeting without any legal reason, and (b) the government forms a committee to plan elected councils in every village. State which concerns a Fundamental Right and which a Directive Principle, with a reason for each.
questions.solution_md: Classify each case and give the reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A **Fundamental Right**: freedom of assembly can be **enforced in court**.
(b) A **Directive Principle**: organising **village panchayats** is a goal the State is guided to pursue, which no court can compel.

questions.stem_md: State two differences between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles.
questions.solution_md: Any two correct differences.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Fundamental Rights are **justiciable** (courts enforce them); Directive Principles are **non-justiciable**.
2. Fundamental Rights are in **Part III** and mostly limit State power; Directive Principles are in **Part IV** and direct the State to act.

questions.stem_md: Some critics say Directive Principles are only hopeful wishes; others say they are a living guide for governments. Give one argument for each view.
questions.solution_md: One argument for each side.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Wishes:** since no court can enforce them, a government may **delay** or **ignore** them.
**Guide:** many laws and programmes have been **based on them**, and the people can **judge** governments by how far they follow them.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by a welfare state?
questions.solution_md: Responsibility for well-being, with examples.

answer.model_answer_md: A **welfare state** is one in which the government takes **responsibility for the well-being** of all citizens, for example through **health, education and social security**, and works to **reduce inequality** and give everyone fair chances.

marking_scheme.step: Government takes responsibility for citizens' well-being
Examples or aims: services, security, less inequality

questions.stem_md: The imagined State of Kaveripur gives free vaccination, pays pensions to the elderly poor and runs free schools. Name two features of a welfare state that these measures show.
questions.solution_md: Link each measure to a feature.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Provision of **basic services** such as health and education to all.
2. **Social security** for those who cannot support themselves, such as the elderly poor, which also helps **reduce inequality**.

marking_scheme.step: First feature linked to a measure
Second feature linked to a measure

questions.stem_md: How does the 73rd Amendment of 1992 carry out a Directive Principle?
questions.solution_md: Amendment and its link to Article 40.

answer.model_answer_md: The **73rd Amendment (1992)** gave **constitutional status** to **panchayats** as units of local self-government. This puts into effect the Directive Principle on **organising village panchayats** (Article 40).

marking_scheme.step: Linked to the principle on village panchayats

questions.stem_md: Name the three common groups into which Directive Principles are classified and give one example of each.
questions.solution_md: Three groups, one example each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Socialistic (economic) principles**, which aim at economic fairness; for example, **equal pay for equal work**.
2. **Gandhian principles**, which reflect village self-rule; for example, organising **village panchayats**.
3. **Liberal-intellectual principles**, which deal with justice, heritage and peace; for example, **separating the judiciary from the executive**.

questions.stem_md: The imagined government of Rajgarh wants to act on three Directive Principles: livelihood for all, village self-government and the protection of national monuments. Suggest one measure for each and name the group it belongs to.
questions.solution_md: A measure and a group for each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Livelihood:** a scheme providing **work and training** (socialistic).
2. **Village self-government:** strengthen **elected village councils** with funds and powers (Gandhian).
3. **Monuments:** a fund and law to **protect and repair** monuments of national importance (liberal-intellectual).

questions.stem_md: A citizens' group in the imagined State of Marunadu asks a court to strike down a State law merely because it does not carry out a Directive Principle on public health. Explain why the court is unlikely to do so, and say what the group can do instead.
questions.solution_md: Non-justiciable; courts act on rights; democratic remedies.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Directive Principles are **non-justiciable**, so a law cannot be struck down only for **failing to implement** one.
2. Courts strike down laws that **violate Fundamental Rights**, not those that merely fall short of Part IV.
3. The group can **campaign**, petition the **legislature** and use **elections** to press for the policy.

marking_scheme.step: Non-justiciable, so no striking down for non-implementation
Courts strike down for rights violation only
Democratic means open to the group

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles in terms of enforceability, nature and purpose.
questions.solution_md: One point each on enforceability, nature and purpose.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Enforceability:** Fundamental Rights are **justiciable**; Directive Principles are **non-justiciable**.
2. **Nature:** Fundamental Rights mostly **restrain the State**; Directive Principles require the State to **take positive action**.
3. **Purpose:** Fundamental Rights secure **political democracy**; Directive Principles aim at **social and economic democracy**.

questions.stem_md: Describe any three features of a welfare state.
questions.solution_md: Any three features.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It provides **basic services**: health care, education and safe living conditions.
2. It offers **social security** such as pensions and help in unemployment, sickness or old age.
3. It tries to **reduce inequality** by giving **equal opportunities** and protecting weaker sections.

questions.stem_md: Show how each of these implements a Directive Principle: (a) the 73rd Amendment of 1992, (b) the Equal Remuneration Act of 1976, (c) the 86th Amendment of 2002 and the Right to Education Act of 2009.
questions.solution_md: Each law linked to its principle.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The **73rd Amendment** strengthened **panchayats**, following the principle on **village self-government**.
(b) The **Equal Remuneration Act** requires **equal pay for equal work** for men and women.
(c) The **86th Amendment** made education a right for children aged **six to fourteen**, and the **Right to Education Act** gave it effect, in line with the principle on **free and compulsory education**.

questions.stem_md: Even though courts do not enforce them, Directive Principles matter to ordinary citizens. Give three reasons.
questions.solution_md: Three reasons.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. They **set goals** that governments are expected to follow in making laws.
2. Citizens can use them as a **yardstick** to judge a government's performance at **elections** and in public debate.
3. Courts may **read them together** with rights when **interpreting** the law, so they influence justice.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following can be enforced by a court of law?

options.text_md: Directive Principles
Fundamental Rights
Both of them equally
Neither of them

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Fundamental Rights. Fundamental Rights are justiciable: a person whose right is violated can approach the Supreme Court or a High Court. Directive Principles are non-justiciable.

questions.stem_md: If a State government violates a citizen's Fundamental Right, where can the citizen go for a remedy?

options.text_md: To the Supreme Court or a High Court
To the Election Commission
To the Rajya Sabha
To the Finance Commission

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** To the Supreme Court or a High Court. The Constitution gives a remedy for violation of Fundamental Rights through the Supreme Court and the High Courts. The Election Commission, the Rajya Sabha and the Finance Commission do not hear such complaints.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined town of Ramnagar, a girl is refused admission to a government school only because of her caste. Her family can approach a court because

options.text_md: the Directive Principles require every school to admit every child
equality and non-discrimination are Fundamental Rights, which courts can enforce
the school has broken a rule of the Election Commission
courts enforce every principle of Part IV

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** equality and non-discrimination are Fundamental Rights, which courts can enforce. Refusing admission on the ground of caste violates the right to equality, a justiciable Fundamental Right. The Directive Principles are not enforceable, the Election Commission has no role here, and courts do not enforce all of Part IV.

questions.stem_md: The imagined government of Pahadgaon announces a plan to protect hill forests and wildlife over the next ten years. Which statement best describes this plan?

options.text_md: It is a Fundamental Right that any citizen can enforce in court
It is illegal because only Parliament may protect forests
It has no connection with the Constitution
It carries out a Directive Principle, which the government is guided but not compelled by courts to follow

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It carries out a Directive Principle, which the government is guided but not compelled by courts to follow. Protecting forests and wildlife is a Directive Principle (Article 48A), so the government acts on a goal that courts cannot compel. It is not a Fundamental Right; a State can act on the subject within its powers; and the plan clearly connects with Part IV.

questions.stem_md: Which description fits the usual nature of Fundamental Rights compared with Directive Principles?

options.text_md: Fundamental Rights mostly limit what the State may do, while Directive Principles ask the State to take positive steps
Fundamental Rights are goals for the future, while Directive Principles protect individuals right now
Both of them are only moral guidance
Fundamental Rights concern only the economy, and Directive Principles concern only politics

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Fundamental Rights mostly limit what the State may do, while Directive Principles ask the State to take positive steps. Most Fundamental Rights act as limits on State power (the State shall not discriminate, shall not deny equality), whereas Directive Principles require positive action such as providing livelihood. The other options reverse or distort this contrast.

questions.stem_md: Which pair correctly states the purpose of Fundamental Rights and of Directive Principles?

options.text_md: Fundamental Rights secure economic democracy; Directive Principles secure political democracy
Both secure only military strength
Fundamental Rights secure political democracy; Directive Principles aim at social and economic democracy
Both are meant only for the courts

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Fundamental Rights secure political democracy; Directive Principles aim at social and economic democracy. Fundamental Rights protect political freedoms and equality, giving political democracy; Directive Principles aim at social and economic democracy. The reversed pair is wrong, and neither concerns military strength alone.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about courts and a State law is correct?

options.text_md: A court can strike down any law that does not carry out a Directive Principle
A court cannot examine any law made by a State legislature
A court can strike down a law that violates a Fundamental Right, but not a law merely because it fails to carry out a Directive Principle
A court can strike down a law only if the Election Commission asks it to

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A court can strike down a law that violates a Fundamental Right, but not a law merely because it fails to carry out a Directive Principle. Courts test laws against Fundamental Rights and may declare a violating law void. Failure to implement a non-justiciable Directive Principle is not a ground for striking down a law. Courts can examine State laws, and they do not need any request from the Election Commission.

questions.stem_md: Two petitions reach a High Court in the imagined State of Eastmoor: (1) traders say a new rule stops them from carrying on their lawful trade; (2) a workers' union asks the court to direct the State to pay a living wage to all workers at once. Which claim can the court examine directly as a legal right, and why?

options.text_md: The traders' claim, because it rests on a Fundamental Right
The union's claim, because Directive Principles are justiciable
Both, because the court enforces all of the Constitution in the same way
Neither, because the court cannot hear claims against a State

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The traders' claim, because it rests on a Fundamental Right. A claim of violation of the freedom to practise a trade rests on a Fundamental Right, which the court can enforce. The living wage is a Directive Principle, which is non-justiciable, so the court cannot direct the State to pay it. Courts do hear claims against a State.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Fundamental Rights mostly act as restrictions on what the State may do.

**Reason (R):** Directive Principles aim at social and economic democracy.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are true, but the aim of the Directive Principles does not explain why Fundamental Rights act as restrictions, so R is not the explanation of A.

questions.solution_md: Rights that courts can enforce are called justiciable.

questions.stem_md: Explain how the nature and the aim of Directive Principles differ from those of Fundamental Rights.
questions.solution_md: Contrast in nature and aim.

answer.model_answer_md: Fundamental Rights mainly **limit the State** and protect individuals, securing **political democracy**. Directive Principles ask the State to take **positive steps** for the people, aiming at **social and economic democracy**.

marking_scheme.step: Aim: political versus social and economic democracy

questions.stem_md: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are called complementary. Explain this with one example.
questions.solution_md: Complementary roles with an example.

answer.model_answer_md: Rights protect individual **freedom and equality**, while the principles aim at **welfare for all**; each completes the other. For example, the **right to education** (a right) and the principle on **free and compulsory education** work toward the same end.

questions.stem_md: Which of these best describes a welfare state?

options.text_md: A state that limits itself to defence and keeping order
A state in which all businesses are closed
A state in which only the army makes decisions
A state that takes responsibility for the well-being of its citizens, including health, education and social security

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A state that takes responsibility for the well-being of its citizens, including health, education and social security. A welfare state promotes the well-being of all citizens through services and security. The second option describes a night-watchman state, and the last two are not forms of welfare state.

questions.stem_md: Which action of an imagined government is the clearest example of welfare-state policy?

options.text_md: Raising an army for defence of the borders
Running free health clinics and giving pensions to elderly people who have no income
Holding an annual trade fair
Building a stadium for national matches

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Running free health clinics and giving pensions to elderly people who have no income. Free health care and pensions for people without income directly promote well-being and social security, the core of a welfare state. Defence, fairs and stadiums have their uses but do not show welfare responsibility.

questions.stem_md: Which promise in the Preamble is most closely linked to the idea of a welfare state?

options.text_md: Justice, social, economic and political
Unity of the nation only
Freedom of trade only
The right to vote only

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Justice, social, economic and political. The Preamble promises justice in its social, economic and political forms, and the Directive Principles are the means of working toward social and economic justice. The other options cover only parts of the Preamble.

questions.stem_md: In 1992 the 73rd Amendment gave constitutional status to panchayats. Which Directive Principle does this carry out?

options.text_md: Equal pay for equal work
Organising village panchayats as units of self-government (Article 40)
Protection of monuments
Separation of the judiciary from the executive

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Organising village panchayats as units of self-government (Article 40). The 73rd Amendment (1992) strengthened village self-government, which is the subject of Article 40. The other options are different principles concerning wages, heritage and the courts.

questions.stem_md: The Equal Remuneration Act of 1976 forbids paying men and women different wages for the same work. Which Directive Principle does it help to realise?

options.text_md: Prohibition of intoxicating drinks
Promotion of international peace
Equal pay for equal work for men and women
Encouragement of cottage industries

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Equal pay for equal work for men and women. The Act gives effect to the principle of equal pay for equal work (Article 39). It has nothing to do with intoxicants, international peace or cottage industries.

questions.stem_md: Which step made education a Fundamental Right for children in the age group of six to fourteen years?

options.text_md: The 73rd Amendment of 1992
The 42nd Amendment of 1976
The Equal Remuneration Act of 1976
The 86th Amendment of 2002, which inserted Article 21A

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The 86th Amendment of 2002, which inserted Article 21A. The 86th Amendment (2002) inserted Article 21A, and the Right to Education Act of 2009 gave it effect. The 73rd Amendment dealt with panchayats, the 42nd with several changes including Article 48A, and the Equal Remuneration Act with equal pay.

questions.stem_md: An imagined State Alpha spends its revenue only on police, courts and defence. Another imagined State Beta also runs schools, hospitals and old-age pensions. What is the difference between them?

options.text_md: Alpha is a welfare state and Beta is not
Both are welfare states in the same way
Neither is a state in the constitutional sense
Beta follows the welfare-state idea of promoting citizens' well-being, while Alpha limits itself to a narrow role

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Beta follows the welfare-state idea of promoting citizens' well-being, while Alpha limits itself to a narrow role. Beta provides services and security that promote well-being, which is the welfare role. Alpha restricts itself to order and defence, a narrow or night-watchman role. The other options reverse or ignore the difference.

questions.stem_md: A law of 2005 promised paid manual work for rural households that ask for it. Which Directive Principle does such an employment guarantee support?

options.text_md: Protection of monuments
Separation of the judiciary from the executive
The right to work, an economic principle
International peace

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The right to work, an economic principle. An employment guarantee supports Article 41 (right to work, within the limits of economic capacity). It does not concern monuments, the courts or international peace.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Directive Principles aim to make India a welfare state.

**Reason (R):** The Directive Principles direct the State to secure social and economic justice for all citizens.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true. Because the principles ask the State to secure social and economic justice, they point the country toward a welfare state.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The 73rd Amendment of 1992 gave constitutional status to panchayats, a step connected with the Directive Principle on village panchayats.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** The amendment strengthened local self-government, in line with Article 40.

The Constitution comes into force with Part IV
The 86th Amendment makes education a Fundamental Right for children
The 73rd Amendment gives panchayats constitutional status
Equal Remuneration Act passed and Article 48A added

questions.stem_md: How is the idea of a welfare state linked to the Preamble and to Part IV?
questions.solution_md: Preamble promise and Part IV goals.

answer.model_answer_md: The Preamble promises **social and economic justice**. The **Directive Principles** in Part IV turn this into goals, such as **livelihood**, education and security, which a welfare state is expected to provide.

marking_scheme.step: Preamble promises social and economic justice
Part IV sets goals toward it

questions.stem_md: Explain how the aim of free and compulsory education for children moved from a Directive Principle to a legal right.
questions.solution_md: Directive aim, 86th Amendment, 2009 Act.

answer.model_answer_md: Education for children was first an **aim of Part IV**. The **86th Amendment (2002)** inserted **Article 21A**, making it a **Fundamental Right** for ages six to fourteen, and the **Right to Education Act (2009)** gave it effect.

marking_scheme.step: 86th Amendment and 2009 Act made it a right

questions.stem_md: Explain in three points how the Directive Principles aim to make India a welfare state.
questions.solution_md: Three links between Part IV and welfare.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. They ask the State to secure a **social order** based on **justice**, social, economic and political.
2. They direct it to provide **livelihood, work, a living wage and public assistance**, reducing hardship.
3. They call for **equal opportunities**, care of **weaker sections**, health and education, lessening **inequality**.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish a night-watchman state from a welfare state, and give one reason why many people prefer the second.
questions.solution_md: Two roles and one reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A **night-watchman state** limits itself to **law and order, defence and justice**.
2. A **welfare state** adds **health, education and social security** and works to **reduce inequality**.
3. Many prefer it because it helps **poorer and weaker citizens** to enjoy a decent life and fair chances.

questions.stem_md:
Directive Principles of State Policy guide those who govern.

(i) What are Directive Principles? Mention where they are found and from which constitution the idea was taken. **[3]**
(ii) Name the three common groups of Directive Principles and give one example of each. **[3]**
(iii) Why are they non-justiciable, and in what sense are they still fundamental in the governance of the country? **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Meaning, source and place; groups; non-justiciable yet fundamental.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) They are **directions to the State** for making laws and policies that bring **social and economic justice**. They are found in **Part IV**, **Articles 36 to 51**, and the idea came from the **Irish Constitution**.

(ii) **Socialistic (economic):** equal pay for equal work. **Gandhian:** organising village panchayats. **Liberal-intellectual:** separating the judiciary from the executive.

(iii) They are **non-justiciable** because the country had limited resources and needed time, so courts were not made to enforce them at once. Still, **Article 37** makes it the **duty of the State** to apply them in making laws, so governments must keep them in view, and citizens can **judge** governments by them.

questions.stem_md:
Directive Principles may be sorted into groups.

(i) State three socialistic (economic) principles. **[3]**
(ii) State three Gandhian principles. **[3]**
(iii) State four liberal-intellectual principles. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Three economic, three Gandhian and four liberal-intellectual principles.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Adequate means of livelihood** for all citizens; **equal pay for equal work** for men and women; the **right to work** and **public assistance** in unemployment, old age and sickness (also a living wage and humane conditions of work).

(ii) Organising **village panchayats**; promoting **cottage industries** in rural areas; promoting the interests of **weaker sections**, including the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (also the prohibition of intoxicating drinks except for medicinal use).

(iii) A **uniform civil code** as a stated goal (Article 44); **separation of the judiciary from the executive**; **protection of monuments** of national importance; promotion of **international peace**; protection of the **environment** (Article 48A, 1976).

questions.stem_md:
Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are both parts of the Constitution.

(i) Distinguish them in terms of enforceability, with the Parts in which they are found. **[3]**
(ii) Explain the difference in their nature and in their purpose. **[3]**
(iii) Explain why it is said that Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles supplement each other. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Enforceability and Parts; nature and purpose; complementarity.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Fundamental Rights** (Part III) are **justiciable**: courts enforce them and can strike down laws that violate them. **Directive Principles** (Part IV) are **non-justiciable**: courts cannot compel the State to implement them.

(ii) Rights mostly **restrain the State**, protecting individual freedom, and secure **political democracy**. Principles require **positive action** by the State and aim at **social and economic democracy**.

(iii) Rights give people **freedom and equality**; principles supply the **welfare** that makes these meaningful. A hungry person cannot use freedom fully, so both are needed. The **right to education** and the principle on **free and compulsory education** point toward the same end, so each **completes** the other.

questions.stem_md:
Three matters come up in the imagined State of Marunadu: (1) a college is refused permission to hold a peaceful procession without any lawful reason; (2) a citizens' forum demands that the government provide work for every unemployed person at once; (3) the government itself proposes a law to organise elected village councils.

(i) Classify each matter as concerning a Fundamental Right or a Directive Principle. **[3]**
(ii) What can a court do, and what can it not do, in these matters? **[3]**
(iii) Why should the government still pursue the matters that courts cannot compel? **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Classification; court powers; why govern by principles.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) (1) A **Fundamental Right**: freedom of assembly. (2) A **Directive Principle**: the right to work and public assistance. (3) A **Directive Principle**: organising **village panchayats**.

(ii) The court can **enforce** the college's right in (1) and strike down an unlawful order. It **cannot compel** the government to provide work in (2) or to pass the law in (3), as these are **non-justiciable**.

(iii) Article 37 makes applying the principles a **duty of the State** in making laws. They express the **goals** of the Constitution: social and economic justice. The people can **judge** the government at **elections**, so ignoring them can be costly, and implementing them moves the State toward a **welfare state**.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) What it cannot do and why

questions.stem_md:
India has set itself the aim of becoming a welfare state.

(i) What is meant by a welfare state? **[3]**
(ii) Mention three activities which a welfare state undertakes for its people. **[3]**
(iii) Explain how the Directive Principles aim to make India a welfare state, with two examples of laws or amendments that carry them out. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Meaning; activities; Part IV and two examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) A **welfare state** takes **responsibility for the well-being** of all its citizens, especially the poor and the weak, and works to **reduce inequality** and give fair chances to everyone.

(ii) It provides **health care**, **education** and **social security** such as pensions and help in unemployment or sickness (also housing and protection of workers).

(iii) The principles direct the State to secure **social, economic and political justice**, a **living wage**, **work**, **public assistance**, equal opportunity and care of weaker sections. Examples: the **73rd Amendment (1992)** strengthened **panchayats**, and the **Equal Remuneration Act (1976)** gave effect to **equal pay for equal work**. The **86th Amendment (2002)** and the **Right to Education Act (2009)** are another.

marking_scheme.step: (iii) Two examples of laws or amendments

questions.stem_md:
The imagined State of Tarangpur has passed a law requiring equal pay for equal work, but some employers say the law is difficult to apply.

(i) Name the Directive Principle behind the law and its group. **[3]**
(ii) Why can a worker not go to court to demand that the State pass such a law? **[3]**
(iii) Evaluate how far laws and programmes of this kind help a country move toward a welfare state, and what else is needed for the aim to succeed. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Principle and group; non-justiciability; balanced evaluation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The principle of **equal pay for equal work** for men and women, a **socialistic (economic)** principle of Part IV; the Equal Remuneration Act of 1976 is an example.

(ii) Directive Principles are **non-justiciable**, so a court **cannot compel** the legislature to make a law to carry them out. A worker can use the law once it is passed, but cannot demand its making.

(iii) Such laws **reduce inequality** and set standards, so they help. But a law alone does not guarantee results: it needs **honest enforcement**, **awareness** among workers, **resources** and **public pressure**. Therefore laws, **fair administration** and **active citizens** must work together before the welfare aim is met.

questions.stem_md:
The imagined government of Chandrapur announces a plan with four measures: (a) a workshop scheme for rural weavers, (b) a pension for destitute elderly persons, (c) a fund to repair a historic fort, (d) free schooling for all children up to the age of fourteen.

(i) Identify the Directive Principle behind any three of the measures. **[3]**
(ii) Name the group to which each of those three belongs. **[3]**
(iii) Explain how the plan moves Chandrapur toward a welfare state, and why a court cannot compel the government to carry it out. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Principles, groups, welfare link and non-justiciability.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) (a) The workshop scheme follows the principle of promoting **cottage industries** in rural areas (Article 43). (b) The pension follows the principle of **public assistance in old age** (Article 41). (c) The fund for the fort follows the principle of **protection of monuments** of national importance (Article 49). [Measure (d) follows the aim of free and compulsory education for children.]

(ii) Measure (a) belongs to the **Gandhian** group; measure (b) to the **socialistic (economic)** group; and measure (c) to the **liberal-intellectual** group.

(iii) The pension and the free schooling give **security and basic services**, the workshops give **livelihood**, and together they help **reduce inequality**, which are marks of a **welfare state**. A court cannot compel the government to carry out the plan because Directive Principles are **non-justiciable**; its execution depends on the **legislature, the budget and the government**, whom the people can judge at **elections**.

children.stem_md: Which feature of Directive Principles does the first speaker rely on?

answer.model_answer_md: That they are **non-justiciable**: courts **cannot enforce** them.

children.stem_md: Name one result the second speaker could cite to show that the principles guide governments.

answer.model_answer_md: **Panchayats** (73rd Amendment, 1992) or **free schooling** for children (86th Amendment and the Right to Education Act).

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Which speaker is more convincing? Give two reasons.
children.solution_md: A supported choice with two reasons.

answer.model_answer_md: The **second** speaker, because the principles **guide law-making** (panchayats, education) and citizens can **hold governments to account** at elections, so they are more than wishes. The first speaker is right on **enforceability** but misses their influence.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Using the debate, state two differences between Directive Principles and Fundamental Rights.

answer.model_answer_md: Fundamental Rights are **enforceable in courts**, whereas the principles are **non-justiciable**. Rights **protect individuals** from the State, whereas the principles **direct the State** to act for social and economic welfare.
